metadata.title: Data Visualization Isn't About Making It Colorful.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: when Claude 'does data visualization,' does that mean picking a colorful palette, or something else first? Lands the carry-out that the chart type comes from the data's relationship, and color only earns a place once it carries meaning.
metadata.anchor_pair: N/A — source is skill-teardown format (anatomy -> pipeline -> constraint -> verdict), no anchor structure to preserve

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes data visualization means picking bright colors. It isn't that — color has to encode something real, and the chart type comes first, chosen from what the data is actually doing.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude, make my chart colorful.', hesitates on 'colorful', corrects to 'accessible'

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 31-word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('colorful'->'accessible') is visible on a late frame.

beats.act: 1 anatomy — a skill is a folder
beats.narration_text: This runs on a skill — a folder Claude reads before it acts. Inside, one file lays out how raw data becomes a chart: pick the chart type for the relationship in the data, write the plotting code, then apply the design and accessibility rules on top. The file is the whole program.

shot.new_visual_element: A folder icon opening to reveal SKILL.md, reference/gotchas.md, reference/examples/; SKILL.md highlighted

production_viz.label: A skill is a folder
production_viz.mechanic: A folder opens on cream to reveal three items: SKILL.md (highlighted in crimson), reference/gotchas.md, reference/examples/. A caption below reads 'Claude reads it, then follows it.'

beats.narration_text: The guide runs both ways. A ranking gets a horizontal bar, a composition over time gets a stacked area, many variables at once get a heatmap. And some charts are ruled out outright: pie charts, because people are bad at comparing angles; three-D charts, because they distort the data; dual axes, because they can imply a correlation that was never there.

shot.new_visual_element: A two-column relationship-to-chart-type list filling in, then a ruled-out-charts list with each entry struck through

production_viz.label: The guide runs both ways
production_viz.mechanic: Top half: a two-column list fills in one row at a time on cream — 'Ranking -> Horizontal bar', 'Composition over time -> Stacked area', 'Many variables -> Heatmap'. Bottom half, boxed apart: a second list appears and each entry is struck through in crimson — 'Pie charts', '3D charts', 'Dual axes'.

beats.narration_text: So color has to earn its place. One accent color carries the finding; everything else fades to grey. Red and green alone are out — about eight percent of men can't tell them apart — and every chart has to survive in black and white: a pattern, a label, a line style standing in for the color, never just decoration.

shot.new_visual_element: A chart where every color drains to grey except one accent bar; a red/green pair marked unreadable; the same chart redrawn with patterns instead of color

production_viz.label: Color has to earn its place
production_viz.mechanic: A bar chart's bars drain from full color to grey one by one, except one bar that stays crimson — the story bar. Beside it, a red swatch and a green swatch sit next to each other with an X over both. Below both, the same chart redraws with hatch-pattern fills instead of color, still legible. Footer: 'Never just decoration.'

beats.narration_text: Data visualization doesn't start with a bright palette — it starts with the chart type the data's relationship calls for, and color only earns a place once it carries meaning.
